title: Reflection starts with interception
question: Can the incident ray reach a receding mirror?
recap: Transform into the mirror’s rest frame, reflect there, and transform back. First check that the light catches the surface: its normal speed must exceed the mirror’s receding speed.
premises: Use an ideal planar perfect reflector with subluminal normal speed.
The incident ray must satisfy c cos φ greater than v.
limitations: At the interception boundary, a tolerance-limited numerical result is not a valid reflection event.
A reflected ray can still have positive laboratory x velocity and separate from a faster receding mirror.

overview.text: Transform into the mirror’s rest frame, reflect there, and transform back. First check that the light catches the surface: its normal speed must exceed the mirror’s receding speed.

full.spoken: The reflected frequency ratio is one minus twice v over c cosine phi plus v over c squared, divided by one minus v over c squared.

full.text: At normal incidence and v = 0.6c, the reflected frequency is one quarter of the incident frequency. The intercepted incident power is 0.4 of the fixed-surface value. With incident energy density u, the pressure is 0.5u. These are different quantities.

The moving-mirror laboratory uses the relative surface-crossing speed, not c by itself, to count intercepted energy. For a ray transverse in the original frame and a mirror receding along positive x, interception fails; the result is not a reflection with zero frequency.

full.returnCaption: Return to can the incident ray reach a receding mirror.

items: Compare the incident normal light speed c cos φ with the mirror speed.
Refuse a reflection event if the ray cannot reach the surface.
Transform the incident wave into the mirror’s rest frame.
Reflect its normal direction there while preserving frequency in that frame.
Transform the reflected wave back to the original frame.
Use the moving-surface crossing rates when comparing incident power, reflected power, and mechanical work.

margin.text: This is an ideal prescribed mirror, not a dynamical model of mirror recoil, absorption, or finite thickness. The source’s pressure unit convention is separate from the SI interpretation used here.
